1:
The chapter opens with a summons unlike anything the divided kingdom had seen in generations: Hezekiah writes to all Israel and Judah, and sends letters expressly to Ephraim and Manasseh, that they should come up to Jerusalem to keep the Passover. The reformed John Gill notes that the king sent not only to his own subjects but to the Israelites of the northern tribes who dwelt within his kingdom, so that none within reach of the call should be left out. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lingers over the very word for "letters," iggeroth, a term of Persian origin used only in late Hebrew, and fixes the date: the first year of Hezekiah was the third of Hoshea, the last king of Samaria, who is described as a better king than his predecessors in 2 Kings 17:2, and who therefore did not actively oppose so national a Passover; the very phrase "to keep the passover unto the LORD" he traces to the law of Exodus 12:48.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses set the political stage. Adam Clarke marvels that such a proclamation was permitted at all, and explains it: Hoshea was among the best of Israel's kings, and by this time the golden calves had been carried off by Assyria — the one at Dan by Tiglath-pileser, the one at Bethel by Shalmaneser — so that those who chose to worship Jehovah at Jerusalem were freely let go. John Wesley reads "Israel" of the men of the ten tribes settled in Hezekiah's kingdom, and the letters to Ephraim and Manasseh as directed to the whole remnant of the north, named by their two chief tribes because they lay nearest and because many of them had long since joined themselves to Judah, as in 2 Chronicles 15:9.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the invitation its heart. The reviving of the temple service had fallen within the season of the feast, and Hezekiah would not let the opportunity cool; so he sent expresses throughout all the tribes, pressing the people to return. In these circular letters, Henry observes, the king discovers a great concern both for the honour of God and for the welfare of a neighbouring kingdom whose prosperity he passionately desired, though it had often vexed his own — and this was rendering good for evil. The design, Henry insists, was not political but pious — "not to bring them back to the house of David, but to bring them back to the Lord God of Israel." "Let them take whom they will for their king," says Hezekiah in Henry's paraphrase, "so they will but take him for their God." The witnesses do not divide: Gill and Wesley fix who was summoned, Ellicott and Clarke the history that made the summons possible, and Henry the generous, evangelical spirit in which a king of Judah flung open the doors of the sanctuary to the estranged tribes of the north.
2:
Behind the invitation lay a deliberation, and the witnesses attend to the council that resolved to keep the feast a month late. The reformed John Gill notes simply that the king, his nobles, and the great senate of the nation consulted together. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fill out the scene: Hezekiah took counsel with his princes and the whole assembly of the capital, gathered in their representatives, to hold the Passover in the second month — a thing the law of Numbers 9:11 permitted to those hindered by uncleanness or by a distant journey from keeping it at the appointed time. Both hindrances, they observe, were present here — the priests unsanctified and the people not yet gathered — the two grounds the law of Numbers 9:6 had contemplated. Over the difficult phrase rendered "sufficiently" they are careful: the word lemaddai means "to sufficiency," and denotes not merely that too few priests had sanctified themselves, but that the priesthood in general had not been consecrated in time.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke names the second month Ijar, and explains the necessity: the purgation of the temple could not be completed until the sixteenth of the first month, so the feast must either be held late or put off a whole year — a delay that would have been fatal to the spirit of reformation now stirring. The law itself, in Numbers 9:10, had allowed those at a distance or accidentally defiled to keep the Passover on the fourteenth of the second month; Hezekiah and his counsellors judged that what was granted to individuals might be extended to the whole people, and the event proved they had not mistaken the mind of the Lord.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees that the resolution was taken by the king in council with his grandees and the popular representatives, apparently before the fourteenth of Nisan, the proper time; the grounds of postponement — the legal impurity of many priests and the non-arrival of the people — are assigned in the verse that follows, and he adds that the first month was Nisan, the Assyrian Nisannu, the second Iyyar, the Assyrian Aru. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way: to keep the feast at its proper time was simply impossible, the temple not yet cleansed nor the people prepared, and so the proviso made for unclean individuals was stretched, by a sound inference, to cover the congregation. The witnesses do not contend; together they show a reformation governed by law even in its urgency — a king who bends the calendar, but only along a seam the law itself had opened.
3:
The verse states the reason the feast could not be held at its ordinary time, and the witnesses weigh the two impediments and a disputed phrase. The reformed John Gill explains that they could not keep it in Nisan on the fourteenth, as the law enjoined, because the cleansing of the temple was not finished until the sixteenth, and to this he adds the two further reasons the text supplies. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the moment precisely: it was the time when the temple had just been reopened, recorded at 2 Chronicles 29:17, its purification not complete until the sixteenth of Nisan; perhaps the Passover would even then have been held, had not the hindrances prevented it. The rare word for "sufficiently," he notes, lemaddai, "unto what was enough," is met with only here, and means that a sufficient number of priests had not sanctified themselves in time to keep the feast in the first month.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, carry the sense forward into the decree it produced, weighing the enigmatic clause "for not in multitude had they celebrated it, as it is written." As early as Rashi this was read to mean that they had not kept it according to the law for a long time — referring the neglect back to the division of the kingdom; but Keil records the objection that this temporal use of the word larob is unusual, and inclines rather to take it of number, the people not "coming in their multitude" to the feast. The two impediments, they add, were distinct and cumulative — the priesthood not consecrated in force enough for the slaying of so many lambs, and the people, scattered through the land, not assembled in Jerusalem at the appointed day.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the "sufficiently" of both manner and number: the priests were not sanctified in such fashion as was fit, nor in such numbers as were needed for the slaying and offering of so many thousands of paschal victims, as the shortage of 2 Chronicles 29:34 had already shown. The witnesses do not divide over the fact — priests unready and people unassembled — though they differ mildly over the last clause, whether it laments a long-neglected feast or a thinly-attended one. What they share is the sober picture of a nation so long estranged from its own worship that even to keep the Passover at all required a month's grace and a general summons.
4:
Brief as the notice is — "the thing pleased the king, and all the congregation" — the witnesses find in it the settling of a weighty question. The reformed John Gill reads the unanimity plainly: they all agreed to it, and determined it should be done. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens what exactly was approved: "the matter was right in the eyes of the king," that is, the twofold proposal to keep the Passover in the second month and to invite the northern tribes to Jerusalem. Both parts of the plan were bold — the one bending the sacred calendar, the other reaching across the old political breach — and both won the assent not of the throne only but of the whole assembly.

That the proposal "pleased" king and congregation alike is, for the witnesses, no idle formality but the visible ground on which the reformation could proceed. Keil and Delitzsch, tracing the decree through these verses, note that the resolution was formally established and proclaimed — the king consulting with his princes and the representatives of the people, and the community giving its voice — so that the keeping of the feast in the second month rested on the shared judgment of the nation. The warrant for that judgment lay in the law itself: the provision of Numbers 9:10 and Numbers 9:11, which had allowed the unclean and the distant to keep the Passover a month late, and which Hezekiah's council now extended, by a sound inference, to the whole congregation.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very brevity of the verse repays a moment's weight. What is recorded here is the moment a plan conceived in the king's chamber became the act of a people: the assembly did not merely submit to a royal order but embraced the proposal as right. It is a small verse, easily passed over; but a reformation imposed only from above rarely endures, and this one, the witnesses show, was owned from below. Gill fixes the unanimity, Ellicott the two things agreed to, Keil the decree it issued in. Between them they show the great Passover carried not by command alone but by consent — a congregation that saw the wisdom of the delay and the grace of the invitation, and made the king's purpose its own. It is the quiet hinge on which the whole solemnity turns, the assent that sets the couriers on the road in the verses that follow.
5:
With the decision made, the machinery of proclamation is set in motion, and the witnesses gather around the herald's cry that would carry the invitation the length of the land. The reformed John Gill reads the establishing of the decree as the passing of a vote that heralds should be appointed and sent throughout the land, that all might know and none plead ignorance. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the phrase more exactly — "they decreed a proposal," and "to make a voice pass" — and observes that the ancient formula "from Dan even to Beersheba" is here reversed to "from Beersheba to Dan," suited to a summons that goes out from Judah northward, as in Judges 20:1.

The crux of the verse is its closing clause, and here Ellicott parts from the older reading. "For they had not done it of a long time in such sort as it was written" he would render rather, "for not in multitude had they kept it, according to the Scripture" — the people had not been in the habit of coming in their numbers to the feast. He points to the law of the Passover in Exodus 12:48 and Deuteronomy 16:1-8, from which it appears the obligation was universal and Jerusalem the only lawful place; and he judges that ever since the division of the kingdom, and perhaps earlier, the Passover had been but inadequately kept, a neglect he ties to the later notice of 2 Kings 23:22. He records the ancient versions too — the Septuagint rendering it well, that a multitude had not done according to the Scripture, while the Syriac and Arabic stray wildly to "because their wealth had grown greatly."

Keil and Delitzsch weigh the same clause and take the same side against an old interpretation. Rashi had read the words temporally — they had not for a long time kept it according to the law, dating the lapse to the schism; but Keil objects that this use of larob of time is unusual, and prefers, with Ellicott, to read it of the multitude that had failed to assemble. So a genuine difference runs beneath the surface: does the verse lament a feast long neglected, or a feast poorly attended? Gill leaves the received sense untouched; Ellicott and Keil press the numerical reading. What none disputes is the melancholy fact the clause records — that the great national ordinance had for generations been kept, if at all, by a thin and scattered few, and that Hezekiah's summons was an attempt to gather, at last, the multitude the Scripture had always intended.
6:
The couriers set out, and the witnesses read both the swiftness of the messengers and the burning appeal they carried: "Ye children of Israel, turn again unto the LORD God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, and he will return to the remnant of you that are escaped out of the hand of the kings of Assyria." The reformed John Gill notes that the posts went through both kingdoms, north and south alike. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the word behind "posts," ratsim, the runners or couriers — men light of foot and trusted, whose office was to carry the royal messages.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain that to the written invitation of the king and his princes the runners were to add words of exhortation, calling the people to turn to the Lord that he might turn to the remnant left them from the hand of Tiglath-pileser and Shalmaneser. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, presses the philology of that "remnant": the word peletah means survivors, as the Assyrian balatu, "to be alive," confirms; and he hears in the whole phrase a rhetorical backward glance to Tiglath-pileser's stripping of Galilee and Gilead, the chronicler's language perhaps coloured too by the memory of Shalmaneser's last fatal inroad in the fourth year of Hezekiah, recorded at 2 Kings 18:9. The couriers themselves, he adds, seem to have been soldiers of the royal body-guard, pressed into the service of the post.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the summons a preacher's whole logic of repentance. The call to "turn again" is a call to conversion, for they had forsaken God and worshipped the calves; and the arguments Hezekiah presses are laid in order — you are children of Israel, and so bound to the God of Israel from whom you have revolted; the God you are called to is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, in covenant with your fathers; and you are but a remnant, narrowly escaped from the kings of Assyria, and therefore the more concerned to put yourselves under the protection of the God of your fathers, lest you be quite swallowed up. The appeal begins and ends, Henry notes, with the promise of mercy: return to him, and he will not turn away his face from you. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke fix the running messengers, Keil and Ellicott the historical weight of "the remnant" and the Assyrian shadow behind it, and Henry the evangelical marrow of the plea — a gospel of return sent, by royal courier, to a people already half-destroyed and still clinging to their idols.
7:
The exhortation turns to warning, holding up the fate of the fathers as a mirror: "Be not ye like your fathers, and like your brethren, which trespassed against the LORD God of their fathers, who therefore gave them up to desolation." The reformed John Gill reads the trespass as the calf-worship and the neglect of the temple service at Jerusalem, and records the Targum's paraphrase, that they "acted deceitfully with the Word of the Lord their God." The sin, then, was no single lapse but the settled apostasy of a whole line — the calf-cultus Jeroboam founded and every northern reign maintained. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott dates the apostasy of "your fathers" from the days of Jeroboam downward, and identifies the "brethren" as the men of Naphtali and the trans-Jordan whom Tiglath-pileser had carried captive; the phrase "gave them up to desolation" he renders "made them an astonishment," echoing the language already used of the land at 2 Chronicles 29:8.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, read the warning in the same key: the fathers and brethren held up as a caution are precisely those already swept away by Tiglath and Shalmaneser, and the desolation named is the visible judgment that fell on their unfaithfulness. The appeal is thus not to abstract fear but to a catastrophe the survivors had watched with their own eyes.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the moral edge, setting this among the arguments Hezekiah urges. "Your late fathers that forsook him and trespassed against him have been given up to desolation; their apostasy and idolatry have been their ruin, as you see — let their harms be your warnings." It is one link in a chain Henry unfolds from the whole letter: that they are children of Israel bound to the God of Israel, that he is the God of their fathers in covenant with them, that their fathers who forsook him were ruined for it, and that they themselves are but a spared remnant. And this argument, the desolation of their brethren, is the most terrible, for it required no faith to see, only eyes to look northward at the smoking ruin of Samaria's countryside. The wreck of the ten tribes is set before the remnant not to crush but to persuade: the very depopulation that had thinned their cities was the sermon God was preaching to those who remained. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the sin and the Targum's gloss, Ellicott and Keil the historical identity of the ruined fathers and the word for their desolation, Henry the persuasive force of a judgment still smoking on the northern hills. The call to return is pressed home by the spectacle of what refusing to return had already cost.
8:
The plea reaches its centre in a cluster of commands — harden not your neck, give the hand to the Lord, enter his sanctuary, serve him, that his fierce anger may turn away. The reformed John Gill glosses "stiffnecked" as obstinate and refractory, like heifers unaccustomed to the yoke that draw back and will not submit. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fasten on the idiom "give the hand to the Lord": it means here not merely to submit, but to give the hand as a pledge of fidelity, the gesture of covenant seen in 2 Kings 10:15, Ezra 10:19, and Ezekiel 17:18. Charles Ellicott renders it "yield ye a hand to Jehovah," a phrase that also means to make an agreement with; the sanctuary he "hath sanctified for ever," as at 2 Chronicles 7:16. He sets the warning "harden not your neck" beside the like charge of Jeremiah 7:26 and the indictment of the northern kingdom in 2 Kings 17:14, where the fathers had done the very thing the sons are now begged to avoid — and he adds, with a critic's candour, that such close resemblances of language betray the somewhat ideal character of these reported addresses.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the giving of the hand into a whole theology of consent. To yield oneself to the Lord is, before communion, to come into covenant; "give the hand" is the word, for a bargain is confirmed by giving the hand — consent to take him for your God, subscribe with the hand to be his, as in Isaiah 44:5, give him your hand in token of giving him your heart. The stiffness Hezekiah warns against is bred in the bone: there is in the carnal mind an obstinacy, an unaptness to comply with God, "we have it from our fathers"; and this must be conquered, the will that had a spirit of contradiction melted into the will of God, the iron sinew of the neck bowed to his yoke. To "enter his sanctuary" is then to attend him in the place he chose, now that its doors are opened and its service revived.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the image of the untamed heifer, Keil and Ellicott the covenant pledge in the outstretched hand and the sanctuary hallowed for ever, Henry the inward surrender that the gesture seals. Together they show the great turning-point of the appeal: not merely to visit Jerusalem, but to strike a bargain with its God — to give the hand, and with it the heart, that the fierceness of his wrath might at last turn away.
9:
The warning gives way to promise, and the witnesses dwell on the tender pledge held out to the penitent: if they turn again to the Lord, their captive brethren and children shall find compassion before their captors and come again to their own land. The reformed John Gill reads "turn again" of turning to the fear and worship of the Lord, as the Targum has it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch spell out the double clause: if ye return, your brethren and your sons who are in exile shall be objects of mercy before those who carried them away, and shall return into this land — the whole grounded in the ancient revelation of God's name in Exodus 34:6, "gracious and merciful." Charles Ellicott confirms the sense of the key word: rahamim, compassion, here the pity a captor is made to feel, as in Psalms 106:46, "he made them objects of pity before all their captors." The pairing "gracious and merciful," he notes, is the standing formula of Nehemiah 9:17, and lives on in the Muslim invocation, "in the name of God the merciful, the compassionate."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reaches, as often, for the Targum, which renders the closing promise finely: the Lord "will not cause his majesty to ascend up from among you, if ye will return to his fear." That majesty, Clarke explains, is the shechinah — the dwelling of the Divine Presence among men, the visible symbol of God with his people; and the pledge is that this Presence, so long provoked, will not withdraw from a people that returns.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a single evangelical maxim that runs through the letters: "If you return to God in a way of duty, he will return to you in a way of mercy." You will find him gracious and merciful, one that will not turn away his face if you seek him, notwithstanding all your provocations; and more, you may hope he will turn again the captivity of your brethren already carried away, and bring them back to their own land. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil fix the conditional promise of a restored exile, Ellicott the pity awakened in the captor's heart, Clarke the abiding Presence that will not depart, Henry the reciprocity of return for return. Together they set before the north the very heart of the gospel Hezekiah preached — that the God against whom they had sinned is swift to show mercy, and keeps the door of restoration open even to a captive remnant.
10:
The couriers pressed on from town to town, and the verse records the bitter reception most of them met: "they laughed them to scorn, and mocked them." The reformed John Gill notes that they were not hindered by Hoshea, one of the better kings of Israel, who was willing enough that his people should go and worship at Jerusalem — a liberty Hezekiah seems to have known when he sent his posts so freely through the northern land. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch defend the phrase "from city to city" against the objection that the kingdom was already ruined: the Assyrians had not blotted out every city nor deported every soul, but had taken the fortresses and carried off the flower of the people, so that many remained in the villages the enemy had spared. The couriers, going among these survivors, met not the silence of an emptied land but the derision of a people who would not be moved.

Charles Ellicott marks the northern limit of the journey, Zebulun, the tribe on the southern border of Naphtali that had suffered under Tiglath-pileser, as Isaiah 9:1 laments; that the messengers reached only so far, and not to Dan, he takes as an incidental note lending an air of historical truth to the account. The verb "laughed them to scorn," he adds, occurs here only, and its tense pictures what the Israelites did continually — a settled, repeated scorn, not a single rebuff. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads "they" of the generality of the ten tribes, who by long famine of God's ordinances had lost their appetite for them, and paid dear for it: about six years after this refusal of grace they were carried away captive, as 2 Kings 18:10 records.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the tragedy home. The messengers went from city to city with pressing entreaties, but the people not only refused, they refused with disdain, abusing those who brought the invitation. Tell them of the God of Abraham — they knew him not; tell them of the sanctuary — their high places were as good; tell them of mercy and wrath — they neither dreaded the one nor desired the other. The destruction of the ten tribes was now but two or three years off; had they accepted the invitation it might have prevented their ruin, but their contempt hastened and aggravated it, and left them inexcusable. The witnesses do not divide: Gill and Keil fix the freedom and the surviving towns, Ellicott and Wesley the reach of the couriers and the nearness of the captivity, Henry the scornful hardness that turned a gospel of life into a savour of death.
11:
Against the general scorn the verse sets a saving exception: "divers of Asher, and Manasseh, and of Zebulun humbled themselves, and came to Jerusalem." The reformed John Gill reads the humbling as a real repentance — they confessed their idolatries and impieties, expressed sorrow, and were now willing to obey God and attend his worship. Their coming was itself a confession, an owning of the God they had abandoned and of the sanctuary they had despised. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that besides these three tribes, the eighteenth verse will add men of Ephraim and Issachar; and since the trans-Jordan and Naphtali had been devastated by Tiglath-pileser, and the couriers went no farther than Zebulun, the roll of responding tribes is exactly self-consistent. The word "humbled themselves," he adds, means simply repented, as at 2 Chronicles 12:6, where Rehoboam and his princes bowed under the threat of Shishak.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, let the fact stand in its plainness: a scattered "divers" out of the northern tribes bowed themselves and made the journey south — a small company against the mocking multitude, but a true one. Nor was the remnant confined to these three tribes, for the account will show men of Ephraim and Issachar among them too, so that from most of the northern tribes at least a few were gathered.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds here the abiding comfort of the passage. "In the worst of times God has had a remnant," and so he had here: some of Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came, that is, were sorry for their sins and submitted to God. The scoffers and the humbled heard the same message from the same messengers; the difference lay wholly within. Henry lays bare the hinge of the whole matter: "Pride keeps men from yielding themselves to the Lord; when that is brought down, the work is done." The difference between the scoffers and the saved was not privilege or opportunity, for both had the same invitation, but the one thing the verse names — humility. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the penitent confession, Ellicott the historical accuracy of the tribes named, Keil the bare and moving fact, Henry the lesson that a humbled heart is the whole of conversion. Where a mocking north turned the messengers away, a lowly remnant took the road to Jerusalem, proof that even in an apostate kingdom under sentence the grace of God was quietly gathering its own.
12:
The scene shifts south, and the witnesses mark a wonder quieter than the northern mockery but greater: in Judah the people were made of one heart. The reformed John Gill traces the unanimity to its source — they were hearty and willing to a man, and this was owing to the power and efficacy of divine grace. The grammatical-historical witnesses press the striking phrase "the hand of God." Charles Ellicott observes that "upon Judah was the hand of God" is here used of a divine influence for good, as in Ezra 8:22, whereas elsewhere the same expression means a judicial visitation, as in Exodus 9:3; the royal command they obeyed was itself "by the word of the LORD," inspired through a prophet — the same coupling of royal command and prophetic word seen at the cleansing of the temple in 2 Chronicles 29:15. Keil and Delitzsch reason the same way: the formula usually carries a punitive sense, but here it is the helping hand of God, working powerfully upon Judah to make them of one mind.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it as the explanation of an astonishing reversal: God, by the power of his grace, inclined the hearts of men lately given up to idolatry to a unanimous compliance with his will and the king's — this is set down as the very reason of the wonderful change wrought in them. The change was the more remarkable, Wesley urges, in men so lately sunk in idolatry, and could be ascribed to nothing but the secret working of God upon the will.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the theology into a sentence. They did it "with one heart," and "the hand of God gave them that one heart; for it is in the day of power that Christ's subjects are made willing." When people show an unexpected forwardness to what is good, we must acknowledge the hand of God in it, "for it is God that works both to will and to do." The witnesses do not divide, and the contrast with the verse before is deliberate and sharp. In the north, the same word of grace met scorn; in the south, it met unanimous consent — and the difference is laid, without embarrassment, to the hand of God, punitive upon the hardened, but here a helping hand that bends a whole people, gently and mightily, into one accord. Gill and Wesley name the grace, Ellicott and Keil the good hand that is elsewhere a hand of judgment, Henry the sovereign power that makes subjects willing.
13:
The day arrives, and the verse simply records the crowd it drew: "there assembled at Jerusalem much people to keep the feast of unleavened bread in the second month, a very great congregation." The reformed John Gill notes only that they came out of the several tribes, north and south together. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the swelling of the assembly into a great congregation, the beginning of the celebration proper. Charles Ellicott fixes the Hebrew behind "much people," larob me'od, "in great multitude" — the very idiom he had weighed at the fifth verse, where the lament was that the feast had not been kept "in multitude"; now, at last, the multitude the Scripture intended is gathered.

That reversal is the quiet point on which the witnesses converge. The feast so long kept, if at all, by a thin and scattered few is suddenly thronged; the word that mourned the empty courts of former Passovers is answered by a congregation "very great." And the second month itself, kept not out of carelessness but by the law's own indulgence for the unclean and the distant, made this crowded feast a monument to a reformation that honoured the law even in the act of bending it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, opening his long meditation on the celebration, seizes on the size and spirit of the gathering as the setting for all that follows. The time appointed having come, a very great congregation assembled, and everything in the account, he says, looks pleasant and lively — a people that had been famished of God's ordinances now crowding to keep them. Henry reads the whole scene as the first fruit of the reformation: the doors of the sanctuary opened, the invitation sent far and wide, and here the harvest of it, a multitude drawn to Jerusalem to eat the Passover. And the gladness, he insists, was no passing holiday mood but the mark of a people restored to communion with their God, forward and lively in a service they had long been strangers to. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the many tribes, Keil and Ellicott the greatness of the congregation and the answered lament of the fifth verse, Henry the gladness and vigour of a nation returned to its feast. What the couriers had carried, and what the hand of God had wrought in Judah and in a northern remnant, now stands visible in one great assembly — the concourse out of which the purifying, the sacrifice, and the joy of the following verses will unfold.
14:
Before a lamb was slain, the people made a stern preparation — they swept the city clean of its idols. The reformed John Gill notes the timing: they arose to this work before they slew and ate the Passover. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the purpose: to purify and sanctify the city for the feast, they removed the illegal altars and incense-places that had been set up under Ahaz, named at 2 Chronicles 28:24, and cast them into the Kidron, as the temple's own defilements had been thrown there in 2 Chronicles 29:16. The word for the incense-places, Keil observes, is here a noun, denoting altars built for the offering of incense. Charles Ellicott adds that Ahaz had reared his altars "in every corner" of the city, and that the term for the incense-burners occurs here only; so that now the city was purified as thoroughly as the temple had been.

The point on which the two grammatical-historical witnesses agree is that the cleansing reached beyond the sanctuary to the streets: a feast to the holy God could not be kept in a city still bristling with the altars of Ahaz, and so the whole capital was purged before the Passover began. As the temple had been cleansed in the first days of the reign, so now the city; the reformation moved outward from the sanctuary, leaving no corner of Jerusalem to its idols.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the act into a gospel lesson. "Before they kept the feast, they cast out this old leaven"; and the application follows at once — "the best preparation we can make for the gospel passover is to cast away our iniquities, our spiritual idolatries." The removing of the altars was not a mere civic tidying but a spiritual reckoning: a people about to feast with God first pulled down the rival worships that had provoked him. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the order of events, Keil and Ellicott the identity of the altars and their casting into the Kidron, Henry the abiding truth the act enshrines. Together they show that the great Passover was prepared for not only by summons and assembly but by demolition — the visible idols of Ahaz flung into the valley, that the city might be clean for the feast, and the reader taught that no communion with God is kept where the old altars are left standing.
15:
The slaying of the lambs begins on the fourteenth of the second month, and the witnesses fasten on the shame that seized the clergy. The reformed John Gill observes that though they could not keep the feast in its proper month, they kept it on the proper day of the month, the fourteenth. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read "the priests and the Levites were ashamed" to mean that under the pressure of a feeling of shame they sanctified themselves and performed their sacrificial duties in the house of the Lord — a shame the more pointed because at the temple's dedication the Levites had outdone the priests in zeal, as 2 Chronicles 29:34 had noted. That earlier passage had praised the Levites above the priests; here, Keil explains, a different company is in view — the priests and Levites who came up from the country, not those already resident in Jerusalem — so the two notices do not clash. Charles Ellicott specifies the object of the shame: they were ashamed of their former reluctance to purify themselves from the defilement contracted under the late reign, and he candidly calls the naming of the Levites here, in the same terms as the priests, a small verbal inaccuracy owing to the writer's wish to be brief.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the shame as the sting of comparison: the negligence and remissness of priests and Levites was upbraided by the general forwardness of the people, and he draws the lesson that "the zeal which we observe in others should make us ashamed of our own coldness, and quicken us not only to do our duty, but to do it with our might."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry paints the scene most vividly. In this celebration the people were so forward and zealous that the priests and Levites blushed to see themselves outdone by the commonalty — the laymen more ready to bring their sacrifices than the ministers were to offer them. This put the clergy upon sanctifying themselves, that the work might not stand still for want of hands. The shame, in Henry's reading, was wholesome: it drove the ministers to the very consecration their office required, so that the people's zeal supplied what the priests' coldness had lacked. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the lawful day, Keil and Ellicott the nature and object of the shame and the small looseness in naming the Levites, Wesley and Henry the goad of the people's zeal. Together they show an unusual reversal in Israel — a laity so eager that its very eagerness rebuked a sluggish priesthood into holiness, and shame itself became, for once, a means of grace.
16:
The sacrifice proceeds in due order, and the witnesses attend to a small but telling irregularity in the handling of the blood. The reformed John Gill notes that the priests stood in their place and the Levites in theirs, each where they were ordered to stand when sacrifice was offered. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the arrangement and its departure from custom: the priests sprinkled the blood of the paschal lambs, receiving it from the hand of the Levites who passed it to them. This was not the ordinary rule, for at the Passover the father of each family who slew his lamb handed the blood to the priest; but here the Levites did it, because — as the next verse will say — many in the assembly had not sanctified themselves, and so the Levites presided over the slaying of the lambs for every unclean person. The blood, they note, was dashed against the altar by the priests alone, but received into their hands from the Levites — an order of ministry devised for the emergency and preserved, the chronicler implies, as the pattern of later Passovers. Charles Ellicott confirms the point: on this occasion the Levites, and not the laymen who brought the victims, slew the lambs and handed up the blood, a breach of the ordinary usage whose reason follows.

Ellicott adds that the phrase "in their place," omdam, is a word used in this sense only in the late books of Daniel, Chronicles, and Nehemiah, and that "after their manner" means "according to their order"; the appeal to "the law of Moses the man of God" is one more of the chronicler's references to the Pentateuchal legislation.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the sprinkled blood to its highest meaning. The priests and Levites did according to the duty of their place, sprinkling the blood upon the altar — "which was a type of Christ our passover sacrificed for us," as 1 Corinthians 5:7 declares. The sprinkling, for Henry, was the beating heart of the rite: not the killing only but the applying of the blood, the very act by which the destroyer had once been turned aside, and by which the true Lamb would one day shelter his people. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the ordered stations, Keil and Ellicott the extraordinary intervention of the Levites and the reason for it, Henry the gospel the blood foreshadowed. Together they show a service conducted "according to the law" and yet stretched by necessity — the Levites stepping into the laymen's office so that the unclean might not be shut out, and the whole rite pointing beyond itself to the true Passover whose blood would one day be sprinkled for a people not yet clean.
17:
The verse gives the reason for the Levites' unusual role: many in the congregation were not sanctified, and so the Levites took charge of killing the Passover for everyone who was unclean, to sanctify the offerings to the Lord. The reformed John Gill explains that a multitude had not been purified from the uncleanness they had contracted, whether by idolatry or by things that under the ceremonial law defiled, and from which they had now no time to cleanse themselves. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the Levites as presiding over the slaying of the paschal lambs on behalf of the unclean, in order to sanctify the lambs to the Lord — for a lamb slain by unclean hands would itself be defiled. So the Levites bore the office of the people, doing for the unclean what the unclean could not lawfully do for themselves. Charles Ellicott notes that the same expedient recurs at the Passover of 2 Chronicles 35:6, but there without apology, as though the precedent set under Hezekiah had become the rule; and he ties the practice to the like ministry of the Levites in Ezra 6:20. The clause "to sanctify them," he adds, refers to the lambs themselves, which would have been ceremonially unfit had they been slain by defiled hands.

The witnesses of the grammatical school thus agree that the whole arrangement was an accommodation to a real and pressing difficulty — a people so long estranged from the legal religion that most of them stood ceremonially unfit to slay their own lambs.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks it plainly as an irregularity, though a pardonable one. The Levites killed the Passover, which by strict law should have been done by the offerers themselves — ordinarily every man killed his own lamb — but now, for those under any ceremonial pollution, the Levites killed it, and assisted more than the law ordinarily allowed in the many purifying sacrifices the occasion required. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the uncleanness and its cause, Keil and Ellicott the sanctifying of the lambs and the precedent that outlived the emergency, Henry the honest acknowledgment that the rule was bent. Together they show a priesthood and a Levitical order improvising, under the eye of the law, to keep the door of the feast open to the unprepared — an irregularity born not of laxity but of mercy, that the unclean multitude might not be turned away from the Passover of their God.
18:
The irregularity now widens from the ministers to the worshippers: a great multitude, many of them from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, ate the Passover though they had not cleansed themselves, and the king rose to pray for them. The reformed John Gill traces the uncleanness to its root — these were of the ten tribes, where idolatry had long prevailed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reckons them the more excusable for coming from countries wholly given to idolatry, and renders the king's prayer from the Targum: "The Lord, who is good, have mercy on this people who err." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that the very naming of the four tribes betrays a documentary source, and that the word for eating "otherwise than it was written" means in illegal fashion, being themselves unclean, contrary to the rule of Numbers 9:6; yet the irregularity was condoned, "for Hezekiah had prayed for them." The phrase "the good LORD" — Jehovah the good — occurs only here, and "pardon" is properly "make atonement on behalf of," as in Leviticus 16:6.

Keil and Delitzsch, correcting the Masoretic division of the verses, read the intercession as one unbroken cry: "May the good Jahve atone for every one" who has set his heart to seek God, though he be not cleansed according to the sanctuary's rule — the prayer running on into the verse that follows.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry probes the pastoral tenderness of the moment. Many were permitted to eat who were not purified to the strictness of the law; it was the second month already, and there was no warrant to defer them to a third, as the first month's law might have allowed. The priests were loth to forbid them altogether, "lest they should discourage new converts, and send those away complaining whom they desired to send away rejoicing." From this Henry, with Grotius, draws the principle that ritual institutions must give way not only to public necessity but to public benefit and advantage. It was Hezekiah's own zeal, Henry adds, that had called them together in such haste, and he would not that any should fare the worse for being straitened of time in their preparation. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke fix the idolatrous background and the plea of excuse, Ellicott and Keil the illegality and the atoning prayer that covered it, Henry the merciful reluctance to turn away the newly returning. Together they show a Passover kept "otherwise than it was written," and a king who, rather than exclude the unready, spread their case before the God who looks on the heart.
19:
The ground of Hezekiah's plea is a principle that pierces to the marrow of true religion: God will pardon everyone "that prepareth his heart to seek God... though he be not cleansed according to the purification of the sanctuary." The reformed John Gill reads it of the worshipper who was heartily desirous of worshipping God and keeping his ordinances, though he adds that Aben Ezra, as Kimchi reports, referred the words rather to Hezekiah himself. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders "prepareth" as "hath directed," and corrects the verse-division that obscures the sense; the construction, he says, is parallel to 1 Chronicles 15:12. What strikes him most is the theology: the prayer "evinces a preference of spiritual sincerity to mere literal observance of legal prescriptions," all the more remarkable as coming from a writer whose chief aim is to foster reverence for the external ordinances of religion. The phrase "purification of the sanctuary," he notes, or "holy purifying," is found nowhere else, and marks the outward, ceremonial cleansing these worshippers had been unable to complete.

Keil and Delitzsch, joining the clause to the intercession before it, take it as the very heart of the king's atoning prayer — that God would cover everyone who had set his heart to seek the God of his fathers, even where the letter of the sanctuary's purification had not been kept.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley distinguishes the two purities in play: "the purification of the sanctuary" is the outward cleansing required of those who came into God's house, named on purpose to set it off against that inward purity the worshippers are here acknowledged to have; and he draws the lesson that "the great thing required in our attendance on God's ordinances is that we prepare our heart to seek him." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the same note into a doctrine of grace: where the heart is sincere there may yet be many defects short of the sanctuary's purity, and these defects, being real sins of omission, need "pardoning, healing grace," to be sought by prayer through the blood of Christ. So a small debate remains — whether the prepared heart is the returning worshipper's or the interceding king's — but the witnesses do not divide on the substance. Gill and Aben Ezra differ on the subject; Ellicott, Wesley, and Henry agree on the sense: that God accepts the heart that seeks him truly, and pardons the ceremonial deficiency a sincere but unready people could not help.
20:
The answer comes in a single clause of striking mercy: "the LORD hearkened to Hezekiah, and healed the people." The reformed John Gill reads it plainly — God heard the prayer, accepted it, and granted what the king desired. The word "healed," however, sets the witnesses to explaining, for no bodily sickness has been named. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch resist the notion that sickness and death were the impending penalty; rather, sin itself was regarded as a spiritual disease, so that "healed" is to be understood of the healing of the soul or of the transgression, as in Hosea 14:4 and Jeremiah 3:22. Charles Ellicott, allowing more to the literal sense, takes the prayer as averting a visitation of divine wrath in the shape of disease and death threatened against uncleanness in Leviticus 15:31, and compares the healing of Abimelech at Abraham's prayer in Genesis 20:17, and the promise of 2 Chronicles 7:14. He gathers a train of like passages where healing is set against uncleanness or sin — the unclean lips of Isaiah 6:5, the backsliding healed in Hosea 5:13 — so that the word carries at once the sense of a plague stayed and a soul restored.

The two grammatical-historical witnesses thus divide gently over the register of the word — Keil hearing a healing of the soul from sin, Ellicott a staying of the plague uncleanness deserved — but both agree that the "healing" is God's gracious acceptance of a people who had come to him unclean.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it simply as pardon: God healed them, that is, pardoned their sin and accepted them and their services as if they had been clean. The healing, on his reading, was pure acceptance — God took the imperfect service as though it had been perfect, for the sake of the sincerity beneath it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, closing his meditation on the prayer, finds in the word a double blessing: the Lord was well pleased with the king's pious concern, and healing "denotes not only forgiveness," as in Psalms 103:3, "but comfort and peace," as in Isaiah 57:18. The witnesses do not divide on the mercy, only on its precise shade. Gill fixes the granted prayer, Keil and Ellicott the meaning of the cure, Wesley the pardon, Henry the peace that followed. Together they show a God who met a technically unlawful worship with acceptance rather than wrath, healing the very people whose uncleanness might have condemned them, because their king had prayed and their hearts had sought him.
21:
The Passover flows into the seven-day feast of unleavened bread, kept "with great gladness," while the Levites and priests praised the Lord day by day. The reformed John Gill notes that the seven days of unleavened bread always followed the Passover, according to the law of Moses. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch puzzle over the odd phrase rendered "with loud instruments unto the LORD," reading it literally as "with instruments of power to the Lord" — that is, instruments with which the singers ascribed power to God; they distinguish the stringed instruments played by the Levites from the trumpets blown by the priests. The daily praise, they note, accompanied the sacrificial service, the great song of thanksgiving falling especially upon the seventh day of the feast. Charles Ellicott renders it the same way, "with instruments of strength to Jehovah," and compares the many psalms that glorify the strength of the God of Israel, such as Psalms 29:1, "ascribe unto Jehovah glory and strength"; yet he grants there is something to be said for the Authorised Version's "loud instruments," since the chronicler elsewhere shows a preference for music loud and strong, as in 2 Chronicles 5:13.

So the two grammatical witnesses offer the reader a choice between two renderings — praise that ascribed strength to God, or praise sounded on strong and pealing instruments — while agreeing that the seven days rang with the daily music of the temple. The chronicler, who loved the temple's song, would have his readers hear these seven days ringing from morning to evening with psalmody.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the plain devotional point. The Levites and priests praised the Lord day by day, both with songs and with musical instruments, thus expressing their own and exciting one another's joy in God; and Henry lifts it into a rule for every age: "praising God should be much of our work in our religious assemblies." The music was not incidental to the feast but part of its very substance, the voice of a joy that could not keep silent; and Henry would have every later congregation learn from it that praise is not the ornament of worship but a chief part of its work. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the law of the seven days, Keil and Ellicott the disputed phrase and the instruments of Levite and priest, Henry the abiding duty of praise. Together they show a feast whose gladness was not silent but vocal and instrumental — a restored temple filled, day after day, with the loud and grateful music of a people who had at last come home to their God.
22:
The king turns encourager, speaking to the heart of the Levites who taught "the good knowledge of the LORD," while the feast ran its seven days with peace offerings and confession. The reformed John Gill reads Hezekiah's words as spoken "to the heart" of the Levites — commending their singing, exhorting them to diligence in teaching, and promising his favour and protection. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch refine the description of these Levites: the phrase is not that they were the more learned in divine things, but that they "showed good understanding in regard to Jahve," having distinguished themselves by intelligent playing to his honour. Charles Ellicott renders it the same way — "showing good skill for Jehovah" in their chanting and playing — and takes "they did eat throughout the feast" to mean that the assembly ate the sacrificial meals furnished from the peace offerings.

Over the closing word, "making confession," a real difference opens. Ellicott insists it here means "yielding hearty thanks," acknowledging the divine goodness, though he grants that everywhere else the Hebrew word means to confess guilt; Keil agrees, taking it neither as confession of sin nor as the bringing of thank-offerings, but simply as acknowledging the Lord with heart and mouth. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it more fully, as a confession of several strands at once — "a religious confession of their relation to God, a penitent confession of their sins and infirmities, a thankful confession of God's mercies, and a supplicatory confession of their wants." So the witnesses genuinely differ: was the people's confession pure thanksgiving, or did it include the acknowledgment of sin?

On the honour done to teaching they are one. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes on the fine phrase "they taught the good knowledge of God to the people," calling it the great work of every faithful minister — to convey that knowledge of God by which men may be saved; and he notes the fatigue and privation the Levites bore, which made the king's kind words the more needful. John Wesley reads their teaching office as the very cause of Hezekiah's respect, and Henry adds that "princes and magistrates, by owning and encouraging faithful and laborious preachers, greatly serve the interest of God's kingdom." Gill fixes the comfort, Keil and Ellicott the skilful praise and the thankful acknowledgment, Henry the fuller confession, Clarke and Wesley the dignity of the teaching Levites — a portrait of a king who strengthened his reformation by honouring its preachers.
23:
Such was the gladness that seven days would not contain it, and the assembly resolved to keep seven days more. The reformed John Gill notes that they consulted among themselves and with the king and his nobles, and all agreed to it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the occasion: the king and the princes had given so large a number of beasts for thank-offerings that there was more than could be used in the seven days of the feast, and so it was resolved to keep the joy for another week of sacrificial meals — against Bertheau, who wrongly supposed the gifts were meant for further separate feasts, when in truth they simply sufficed for a second seven days. The word rendered "gave," Keil notes, means to set apart or bestow as a heave-offering, so that the surplus of the princes' bounty overflowed naturally into a second week of feasting. Charles Ellicott reads "took counsel" as "determined," the result of taking counsel, and compares the double week of Solomon's dedication in 2 Chronicles 7:9; he notes how fond the chronicler is of dwelling on the joy of the ancient festivals, as if to press greater whole-heartedness upon the people of his own day.

That fondness for the festival's joy is the note on which the grammatical witnesses and the Puritan meet. The prolongation was no new institution but an overflow of gladness the ordinary term could not hold.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry enters into the mood of it. Having kept the seven days in a religious manner, they had so much comfort in the service that they kept other seven; they did not invent any new modes of worship, but repeated and continued the old. The case was extraordinary — long deprived of the ordinance, they knew not when they might have such another opportunity, and could not find in their hearts to separate till they had doubled the time. Many were far from home, and it was harvest, this being the second month; yet they were in no haste to return, for "the zeal of God's house made them forget their secular affairs." How unlike, Henry adds, those who snuffed at God's service, and asked when the sabbath would be gone. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the counsel, Keil and Ellicott the abundant gifts and the chronicler's love of festal joy, Henry the holy reluctance to disperse. Together they show a people so glad in recovered worship that they willingly kept a second feast upon the first, harvest and homes forgotten in the joy of the Lord.
24:
The prolonged feast was made possible by a royal and princely liberality, and the witnesses reckon its scale and its grace. The reformed John Gill explains that Hezekiah separated the beasts from his own herds and flocks, or purchased them at his own charge, lifting them up as heave offerings to the Lord and giving them to the people for thank-offerings to feast upon. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set down the sums — a thousand bullocks and seven thousand sheep from the king, a thousand bullocks and ten thousand sheep from the princes — and note that they were so abundant that they sufficed not only for the feast itself but for the added week. The verb for the giving, they add, is that of a heave-offering set apart to God, the same generosity the princes matched and exceeded in their gift of small cattle. Charles Ellicott renders "did give" as "had presented," for sacrifice as a terumah or heave offering, and fastens on the closing clause: "priests had sanctified themselves in multitude." The priests no longer hung back as they had done at first, in 2 Chronicles 29:34 and again at the opening of the feast; now there was no lack of persons duly purified for the sacrifice of so many victims.

That reversal in the priesthood is the quiet gain the witnesses mark: the reluctance that had shamed the ministers early in the feast has given way, under its infectious joy, to a ready and ample consecration.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley weighs the king's generosity and finds it the more considerable for its timing. Hezekiah gave first to God, to whom the appointed parts were offered in thanksgiving, and then to the people, who feasted on the remainder as the offerer used to do in peace-offerings, giving away his own right in the relics. And this open-handedness came at the very beginning of his reign, when he found the exchequer empty, and had already been at great expense in cleansing and refitting the temple and preparing for the feast. That a king should give so freely from an emptied treasury, at the very outset of his reign, Wesley reckons the surest proof of the piety that moved him. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the heave-offering from the king's own stock, Keil the abundant sums, Ellicott the priests at last sanctified in number, Wesley the costly generosity of a king newly come to an emptied treasury. Together they show a reformation sustained not by decree alone but by sacrifice — a prince impoverishing himself to feast his people before the Lord, and a priesthood finally rising, in full strength, to the work.
25:
The joy of the feast is now numbered by those who shared it, and the witnesses count the ranks of the rejoicing. The reformed John Gill sets first the congregation of Judah, gathered out of its several cities — the largest company — joined by the priests and Levites who dwelt in Jerusalem. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out three groups that took part: the whole congregation of Judah with its priests and Levites; the whole congregation of those who had come out of Israel, the ten tribes; and the strangers, both those who came from the land of Israel and those already dwelling in Judah. The joy, they stress, was shared without distinction of origin, the reunited nation and its guests rejoicing together in one house. Charles Ellicott sharpens the last class: the "strangers," gerim, are the proselytes, and he is careful to distinguish the word from the garim of the earlier migration under Asa in 2 Chronicles 15:9, pointing rather to the law of the stranger in Leviticus 17:12.

On the identity of these strangers the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is precise: they were "proselytes of the covenant," Gentiles who had embraced Judaism and submitted to the rite of circumcision — for none others, he insists, could be permitted to eat the Passover at all. The rejoicing multitude, then, was not a loose crowd but a company every part of which had a right to the feast: native Judah, returning Israel, and the circumcised proselyte alike.

The witnesses do not divide, and their careful enumeration carries its own quiet theology. The feast that Ahaz had let fall, and that generations had kept only by a scattered few, now drew together Judah and Israel and the stranger into one glad assembly — the divided nation and the incoming Gentile met at a single table. It is the same breadth the prophets would one day promise, when the nations should come up to keep the feast; here, in a Passover of the eighth century before Christ, its first small earnest appears. Gill fixes the great body of Judah, Keil the three participating groups, Ellicott and Clarke the proselytes who by circumcision had earned their place. Together they show the breadth of the joy: a Passover that gathered not only the reunited tribes but the outsider who had joined himself to the covenant, a foreshadowing, in the recovered feast of a divided people, of a wider ingathering yet to come.
26:
The verse crowns the account with a superlative: "since the time of Solomon the son of David king of Israel there was not the like in Jerusalem." The reformed John Gill is careful that the joy was not merely carnal, expressed in eating and drinking, but spiritual, springing from the restoration of the temple service and the feasts of the Lord. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the comparison with Solomon: this feast could be matched only by the dedication of the temple in 2 Chronicles 7:1, in respect of its length, the richness of its offerings, the multitude that shared it, and the joy that marked it. That dedication had itself run fourteen days, the feast of tabernacles following hard upon the seven days of the proper dedication; and since Solomon's day all the tribes had never been united at a feast in Jerusalem. Charles Ellicott reads it the same way, noting that the chronicler himself draws the parallel with the twofold Feast of the Dedication, and citing Bertheau that no festival since Solomon could compare with this in duration, abundance of sacrifices, number of participants, or joy.

The point on which the grammatical witnesses converge is the sheer span of years the comparison reaches back across — the better part of three centuries, the whole age of the divided kingdom, in which no such gathering had been seen.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes why the interval was so long and so barren: from the days of Solomon the ten tribes had been separated from the true worship of God, and now, for the first time, many of them — from Asher, Issachar, Ephraim, Manasseh, and Zebulun — had joined to celebrate the Passover. That, for Clarke, is the marvel the verse records: not merely a large or a happy feast, but the first reunion of north and south at the altar in living memory. It was, in his eyes, the reversal of the whole tragedy of the schism, however brief it proved. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the spiritual quality of the joy, Keil and Ellicott the measure of the comparison with Solomon's dedication, Clarke the healing of a schism three hundred years old. Together they show why the chronicler reached for the greatest name in Jerusalem's history to describe it: since the golden age of the temple's founding, the holy city had not known a gladness so deep or so wide.
27:
The great assembly is dismissed with a blessing, and the chapter closes on the ascent of that blessing to heaven: "their voice was heard, and their prayer came up to his holy dwelling place." The reformed John Gill notes that the priests who blessed were of the tribe of Levi — unlike the counterfeit priests of the northern kingdom, drawn from any of the people — and that while the priests pronounced the blessing the Levites might well have been singing. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the historian's closing sentence as a considered inference: from the divine blessing resting on the festival, traceable in the zeal the people afterward showed for the temple worship in 2 Chronicles 31 and in the deliverance of Judah from the Assyrian Sennacherib in 2 Chronicles 32, the writer concludes that the priests' prayer had indeed reached God's holy dwelling. Charles Ellicott confirms that these were "the Levitical priests," not irregular ministrants, and that the priestly blessing was itself a prayer that Jehovah would bless, prescribed in Numbers 6:23; that it was heard, the writer gathers from the progress of reform and the wonderful rescue from Assyria, and Ellicott marks the characteristic omission of the sacred Name in the phrase "his holy dwelling place."

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses close the chapter on differing notes. John Wesley observes simply that the blessing belonged to those Levites who were also priests, for to them alone this work pertained. Adam Clarke, however, turns from the ascended prayer to a mournful reflection: God accepted the fruits of the pious disposition he had himself infused, and their prayer rose like the smoke of their sacrifices; yet how soon were these bright prospects beclouded. It is not for want of holy resolutions or heavenly influences that men are lost, Clarke insists, but through their own unsteadiness — they do not persevere, the Holy Spirit is grieved and departs; and he presses the point to its sharpest edge, that those who draw back to perdition truly had saving grace, "showed it, trifled with it, sinned against it," and are therefore lost. It is a distinctly Arminian warning, wrung from a chapter of unmatched joy.

The witnesses do not finally divide over the verse itself. Gill fixes the lawful priesthood, Keil and Ellicott the blessing that ascended and the later mercies that proved it heard, Wesley the priestly office, Clarke the solemn caution against falling away. Together they end the chapter where it began — with prayer rising from Jerusalem toward heaven — and let the reader see that the same God who healed an unclean people and gathered a divided nation sent them home under a benediction that reached his holy dwelling-place, even unto heaven.
